additions.title: Essop and others v Home Office (UK Border Agency); Naeem v Secretary of State for Justice [2017] UKSC 27
additions.publisher: UK Supreme Court, published by The National Archives (Find Case Law)
additions.quote: it is commonplace for the disparate impact, or particular disadvantage, to be established on the basis of statistical evidence
additions.why: The leading UK authority on what a disparity proves. The Supreme Court held that a claimant need not show why a practice disadvantages a group: the statistics can establish particular disadvantage on their own, leaving the organisation to justify the practice. In Essop the pass rate for one group was 40.3% of another's, with a 0.1% likelihood of that arising by chance. Not an AI case (a staff promotion test and a pay scale), and it sets no numerical threshold. It fills a gap the research log recorded: no UK case law had been read.

additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by The National Archives (Find Case Law)
additions.quote: SWP have not done all that they reasonably could to fulfil the PSED
additions.why: A UK court finding against a deployer for not testing. The police force had never sought to satisfy itself, directly or by independent verification, that the facial recognition software had no unacceptable bias on grounds of race or sex, and the supplier's refusal to share training data on grounds of commercial confidentiality was no answer. Rests on the public sector equality duty, so it binds public authorities; the court did not find that the software was biased.

additions.title: Equality Act 2010, section 136: Burden of proof
additions.quote: If there are facts from which the court could decide, in the absence of any other explanation, that a person (A) contravened the provision concerned
additions.why: Why test results matter in a claim. Once the facts could support a finding of discrimination, the court must make that finding unless the organisation shows otherwise. An organisation that has never measured outcomes by group has little to show. The section does not mention statistics or testing; that reading is ours, drawn from how the section and Essop fit together.

additions.title: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 9: Risk management system
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
additions.why: The one binding rule read that requires thresholds to be fixed before testing, which the research log could not source. Testing must also happen before a system is placed on the market or put into service. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. EU law, on providers of high-risk systems; the article covers risk testing generally and does not name bias. No direct effect in the UK. Application dates are not stated here.

additions.title: Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (1978), 29 CFR 1607.4: Information on impact
additions.publisher: US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; Code of Federal Regulations, US Government Publishing Office (govinfo.gov)
additions.locator: s.1607.4(D), 'Adverse impact and the four-fifths rule' (p. 222 of the 1 July 2024 edition)
additions.quote: where the differences are based on small numbers and are not statistically significant
additions.why: The original of the four-fifths rule in the brief's figure, which the first pass saw only as quoted by NIST. The text shows it is a general guide for United States enforcement agencies ('will generally be regarded' as evidence of adverse impact), not a pass mark: smaller differences may still count where statistically and practically significant, and larger ones may not where numbers are small. United States federal guidelines for employment selection, dated 1978; no force in the UK. This is the 2024 annual edition; the live eCFR site refused automated reading.

additions.title: Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT): Local Law 144 of 2021
additions.publisher: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
additions.quote: unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of the use of the tool
additions.why: International comparator: a law that makes a bias audit within the past year, with information about it made public, a condition of using an automated employment decision tool. It is the closest thing in force to the criterion's top level, where testing is independently audited and results are made public. New York City employers and employment agencies only; enforced from 5 July 2023. The enforcing department's summary page; the text of the law and the rule were not read.

additions.title: Universal Credit Advances Model: Fairness Assessment (1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025)
additions.quote: Due to the limited availability of protected characteristic data for the high-risk cohort, age is the only protected characteristic that has been measured.
additions.why: A published UK bias test of a live machine learning system, and a candid example of its limits. The department defines two disparity measures, reports the results and concludes there are minimal concerns, but could measure only one protected characteristic, age, for lack of data. It found inconsistencies for some age groups, which it says retraining may reduce, and that non-UK nationals were more likely to be referred by the model than UK nationals (para 21). The department's assessment of its own model, not an independent audit.

additions.title: Summary: accuracy and equitability evaluation of Cognitec FaceVACS-DBScan ID v5.5 (National Physical Laboratory testing of the facial recognition algorithm used to search the Police National Database)
additions.locator: Sections on what the testing found and how policing and the Home Office responded
additions.quote: the testing identified that in a limited set of circumstances the algorithm is more likely to incorrectly include some demographic groups in its search results
additions.why: What independent testing can find in a system already in use: the National Physical Laboratory's tests showed the police's retrospective facial recognition algorithm was more likely to return wrong matches for some demographic groups at the operational setting. The Home Office says it has procured and tested a replacement and reissued guidance. This is the Home Office's summary; the laboratory's full report (PDF) was not read, so no figures are given. Law enforcement use only.

additions.title: Review into bias in algorithmic decision-making
additions.publisher: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation
additions.quote: the four-fifths rule is not part of UK law, and not a meaningful test of whether a system might lead to discrimination under UK law
additions.why: A UK official source for the caution in the brief's figure, in stronger terms than the brief uses: the review found many suppliers applying the United States four-fifths rule and said it is not a meaningful test under UK law. It also says the only way to be sure a model is not discriminating is to check, which needs demographic data. Advisory; 2020.

additions.title: Introduction to AI assurance
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
additions.quote: A third-party auditor works with internal staff to define the scope and objectives for the audit.
additions.why: The government's plain-language definition of a bias audit and a worked example of one done by an outside auditor on a recruitment sifting tool, where the audit finds that home address is acting as a stand-in for protected characteristics. Read in the first pass but left off the list for space. Guidance, not a requirement; the example is a worked illustration.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (US)
additions.quote: Fairness and bias – as identified in the MAP function – are evaluated and results are documented.
additions.why: The widely used voluntary framework makes evaluating fairness and bias, and keeping the results, a named outcome. A benchmark for 'results recorded'. Voluntary; United States; it sets no metric or threshold.

additions.title: IEEE 7003-2024: IEEE Standard for Algorithmic Bias Considerations
additions.locator: Standard summary on the IEEE Standards Association page
additions.quote: criteria for the selection of validation data sets for bias quality control
additions.why: The international technical standard on algorithmic bias, approved in December 2024. Its published summary says it covers how to choose validation data for bias checks and how to set and communicate the boundaries within which an algorithm has been validated. Only the standard-setter's free summary was read; the standard itself was not opened, so nothing is claimed about its detailed requirements. Voluntary.

additions.title: Research Note: A literature review on bias in supervised machine learning
additions.quote: one useful notion of bias is conditional demographic disparity
additions.why: The financial regulator's staff review of how bias is measured. It says the available metrics reflect different ideas of fairness and points to conditional demographic disparity, which compares outcomes for groups among people with the same relevant characteristics, as one useful measure. A research note that states it may not represent the FCA's position; not guidance, and no threshold is proposed.

additions.title: Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores
additions.publisher: Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan and Manish Raghavan (arXiv; Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science 2017)
additions.quote: key notions of fairness are incompatible with each other, and hence provide a framework for thinking about the trade-offs between them
additions.why: The mathematical result behind 'thresholds chosen and justified in advance': except in special cases, a risk score cannot satisfy several common fairness conditions at once. So an organisation has to decide which measure it is testing against and say why, before it looks at results. Theoretical paper, not an empirical study; authors' preprint of a conference paper. Only the abstract was read.

additions.title: The four-fifths rule is not disparate impact: a woeful tale of epistemic trespassing in algorithmic fairness
additions.publisher: Elizabeth Anne Watkins, Michael McKenna and Jiahao Chen (arXiv preprint)
additions.quote: This metric incorrectly introduces a new deontic nuance and new potentials for ethical harms that were absent in the original 4/5 rule.
additions.why: Research support for treating the four-fifths ratio with care: the authors trace how one part of United States law was turned into a single software metric and built into fairness toolkits, losing the legal context. Preprint, not confirmed as peer reviewed; United States law; an argument, not a measurement. Only the abstract was read.

additions.title: Fairness Under Unawareness: Assessing Disparity When Protected Class Is Unobserved
additions.publisher: Jiahao Chen, Nathan Kallus, Xiaojie Mao, Geoffry Svacha and Madeleine Udell (arXiv; ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency 2019)
additions.quote: Empirically, these methods are observed to exaggerate disparities, but the reason why is unknown.
additions.why: Evidence on testing with guessed characteristics. Where group membership is inferred from proxies such as surname and location, the measured disparity is biased, generally upward for the common method, by an amount that depends on the cut-off used. It supports the regulator's finding that inferred data is not accurate enough to monitor bias. Tested on simulations and a public dataset of mortgage applications; authors' preprint of a conference paper. Only the abstract was read.

additions.title: Mitigating Bias in Algorithmic Hiring: Evaluating Claims and Practices
additions.publisher: Manish Raghavan, Solon Barocas, Jon Kleinberg and Karen Levy (arXiv; related DOI 10.1145/3351095.3372828)
additions.quote: document what they have disclosed about their development and validation procedures, and evaluate their practices, focusing particularly on efforts to detect and mitigate bias
additions.why: An academic study of what suppliers of pre-employment screening algorithms say publicly about how they validate their tools and test for bias. Background for the criterion's top level, where methods are published to buyers. Based on what vendors have disclosed, as at 2019; authors' preprint. Only the abstract was read.

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/201.quote: A cannot show it to be a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim

https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-.quote: The frequency of the monitoring should be proportional to the impact of incorrect outputs on individuals and vulnerable groups.
you could use the dataset to test how your system performs with different groups, and also potentially to re-train your model to avoid discriminatory effects

https://www.gov.uk/government/publicatio.quote: Bias audits should be repeated at regular intervals after the system is in operation to ensure consistent performance.

https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Specia.quote: The plethora of fairness metric definitions illustrates that fairness cannot be reduced to a concise mathematical definition.

rejected.reason: Returned a 'Request Access' page ('Due to aggressive automated scraping'). Not bypassed. The same section was read in the Government Publishing Office's 2024 annual edition instead.

rejected.title: Equality and Human Rights Commission, Artificial intelligence in public services
rejected.reason: Tried again on 5 October 2026: HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare browser challenge. Not bypassed, not read, not cited. The CDEI review (added) records that it asked the Commission for guidance on how the Equality Act applies to these tests.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC TR 24027:2021 (bias in AI systems) and ISO/IEC TS 12791:2024 (treatment of unwanted bias)
rejected.reason: ISO's own pages return 403 (browser challenge). Sold standards with no readable free page, so nothing is cited. IEEE 7003-2024 is cited from its free summary instead.

rejected.title: Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell, Why Fairness Cannot Be Automated (arXiv 2005.05906)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). Relevant here for its proposed measure, conditional demographic disparity, but already placed under discrimination risk awareness; the FCA research note (added) covers the same measure.

rejected.title: Report: accuracy and equitability evaluation of Cognitec FaceVACS-DBScan ID v5.5 (National Physical Laboratory, full report)
rejected.reason: Not opened in this pass; the Home Office summary page was read and cited. The full report holds the error rates by demographic group and should be read before any figure is quoted.

rejected.title: Chouldechova, Fair prediction with disparate impact (arXiv 1610.07524)
rejected.reason: Reachable. Makes the same point as Kleinberg and others on incompatible fairness measures; one is enough.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief; three sources would strengthen it. (1) The research log said no UK case law had been read on what disparity counts: Essop v Home Office [2017] UKSC 27 (paras 24-28) holds that statistical evidence alone can establish particular disadvantage, without showing the reason for it. (2) The log could not source 'thresholds set in advance' as a requirement: EU AI Act Art. 9(8) requires testing 'against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds' (EU, high-risk providers only). (3) On the brief's figure, the CDEI review goes further than the brief, calling the four-fifths rule 'not a meaningful test' under UK law, and the original United States text (29 CFR 1607.4(D)) shows it was never a pass mark. One wording point: the Supreme Court itself uses 'disparate impact' alongside 'particular disadvantage', so the term is not purely American, though the statute's words remain 'particular disadvantage'.
